It is only after the results have been released that they come back home. Some may have not been back since then, and that is a fact. Mr Speaker, aside that, I have seen the prospectus, and my Colleagues have taken us through the prospectus. One will need over GH₵7000. We recognise that they are not paying tuition fees. One would need GH₵5,000 to GH₵8,000, depending on what one is buying. It will be wrong for us in this Chamber to assume that because we can afford GH₵5,000 easily, everybody out there can afford GH₵5,000 in days. We all know the state of the economy. Even us, we are among only about 0.1 per cent of the population. So, if one is to take the population of 35 million, MPs here are among the privileged 0.1 per cent. That is approximately 3500 people. So, if they can afford it, it does not mean their constituents can afford it in days. topk.text: Benign visible content about education policy, school access, and constitutional education rights.

education. It is emphatic that basic education should be compulsory for every child of school going age. However, the focus on the SHS level at the expense of the basic level in recent times, motivated by the Free SHS policy has further exacerbated the deterioration of quality education in the country. Mr Speaker, the perceived prevailing climate of fear and intimidation has restricted the ability of school administrators to voice out their concerns regarding the declining quality of education. Many headteachers and principals feel constrained and unable to express their grievances openly for fear of losing their jobs. Consequently, the lack of constructive dialogue and effective problem-solving within the educational system has untold negative repercussions on quality education in the country. Mr Speaker, Parent-Teacher Associa- tions (PTAs) hitherto, played a crucial role in supporting Government in the running of schools. PTAs have been instrumental in providing school needs, including infrastructure, vehicles, motivation of staff and other administrative needs of schools. However, due to perceived political expedience by Government, schools have been cautioned not to allow parents to contribute towards school development. It is sad to note that some heads were reprimanded for asking parents to pay PTA levies. The decision to stop parents from contributing towards their children’s education has run down some schools drastically because PTAs remained the backbone of the development of some schools. Mr Speaker, Ghana’s international reputation in the field of education has suffered a setback due to the pervasive decline in standards, diminishing the country’s credibility and competitive- ness on the global stage. According to the 2018 World Development report, Ghana has been ranked second to last in education globally. This has placed Ghana among the worse countries on education worldwide, an alarming cause to worry about. Besides, Ghana’s educational system risks producing half-baked graduates whose performance is likely to affect us in diverse forms, socially, economically, culturally, health-wise and even in sustainable development. In addition, our hope of transforming Ghana into an industrial nation is likely to suffer setbacks as a result of the poor quality of education if care is not taken. 45 6th December, 2023 46 Statements Mr Speaker, urgent measures must be implemented to address the critical issues plaguing the Ghanaian educational system. Immediate attention should be directed towards revitalising the neglected basic education level, including the provision of essential resources and infrastructure, such as teachers, school buildings, furniture, teaching and learning materials, among others. Mr Speaker, Government, as a matter of urgency, must free the PTAs to do their work. Empowerment of PTAs must be facilitated to enable their active participation and support in the educational sector. It is a fact that Government alone cannot shoulder the burden of education, hence a collaborative approach between the Government and PTA is more sustainable and the way to go. Mr Speaker, it is imperative for Government to prioritise the educational sector by fulfilling its commitments and allocating sufficient resources to ensure the effective functioning of educational institutions. Revising the existing promotion and demotion policies within the educational system could foster a more conducive environment

Leave the rest of the procedure to the Chair. I have given you the— Dr Mahama: Mr Speaker, thank you very much for that direction, but I was just trying to help guide the Chair. Mr Speaker, the maker of the Statement brought to the fore the issue about education and education at the crossroads. He highlighted some of the teething issues regarding Ghana’s educational system. He also brought to our attention some of the sterling, most innovative and cutting-edge educational initiatives that were initiated by the former President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo. But the most important thing in that Statement to me that should engage our minds, is his comment on the flagship programme of the previous Government that is, the Free Senior High School (FSHS) Programme. Mr Speaker, I have had the opportunity of writing some papers on education. I remember when I was reading my second degree, I wrote about gender inequalities in primary school enrolments and the factors that probably would necessitate or determine whether a person would enroll a female or a male student in school. One of the findings was the financial status of the parents. The FSHS basically took away this burden and made education accessible to every Ghanaian, irrespective of where one was born or the financial status of their parents. I think that this Programme would have to be safeguarded. It is in tandem with the provision of Constitution of the Republic that states that education should be progressively free. Any attempt by any government to introduce any impediment to the access to education by way of parents paying, would not be in furtherance of 123 19th February, 2025 124 Statements the Constitution of the Republic of the country. Mr Speaker, there are recent talks about parents having to pay for some part of Parent-Teachers’ Association dues. There are recent talks about engagement with institutions to ensure that education is actually being contributed to by parents. The FSHS legislation could not be passed by in the previous Parliament. This Parliament would have to pass it, ring- fence funding sources for education and make sure that it is accessible for everyone. Mr Speaker, thank you. Mr Second Deputy Speaker: Thank you very much. I would take the last comment. So, I would give it to either the former Minister or— Prof Nyarko: Please, I am indulging you to indulge the two of us, with respect to your office. Mr Second Deputy Speaker: Please, we all know that the Statement that has been read is a very important Statement that we need to discuss. But our own Colleague raised the issue of quorum. So, with the ten minutes I have, I have to make sure that—Please, I am going by my own time. So, Prof Kingsley Nyarko, let me hear you. Prof Kingsley Nyarko (NPP — Kwadaso): Mr Speaker, you are a nice man. Thank you for the opportunity you have given to me. They also mentioned that the programme had taken away the financial burden on parents, making education more accessible [09e40dc218eabe6140d3da9f41fa5089177303b29afff412bbf04b7939384856:52].
